name: FirstWeek
description: An AI-powered project onboarding platform with source-grounded answers and project-scoped access. Phase 1 is complete; further features are in active development.
longDescription:
## Overview

FirstWeek helps new team members understand an unfamiliar codebase without having to piece together scattered documentation or rely on unverified AI answers. It combines a project onboarding workspace with conversational RAG, visible citations, architecture diagrams, and clear company and project boundaries.

## Current status

**Phase 1 is complete, and the project remains in active development.** The first phase establishes the core onboarding experience and technical foundation. I plan to expand the product through additional phases as I learn from real onboarding workflows and add more useful collaboration features.

## System architecture

```text
New team member
       │
       ▼
React / Vite workspace
  ├── project directory
  ├── reading guides
  ├── architecture views
  └── conversational Ask
       │
       ├──────────────► Express auth service
       │                  └── PostgreSQL users + project ACL
       │
       ▼
Express chat + recall services
       │
       ▼
Python / LangGraph RAG engine
  ├── hybrid retrieval
  ├── graph context
  └── source-grounded generation
       │             │
       ▼             ▼
 Neo4j graph    Embedding service
       │
       ▼
Cited answer + inspectable source reader
```

## What Phase 1 delivers

- A membership-protected workspace for project overviews, reading guides, architecture, and team context.
- Conversational questions answered from indexed project knowledge with visible supporting sources.
- Project-level access control and multi-tenant data boundaries.
- Source-backed visual architecture diagrams.
- English and Japanese interface support.
- Local and containerized workflows for indexing, retrieval, and full-stack development.

## Next phases

FirstWeek is intentionally not presented as finished. Future phases will deepen the onboarding workflow, improve how teams curate and maintain knowledge, and add features based on practical use. The existing service boundaries and provider factories are designed to let those capabilities grow without coupling the interface to one model or retrieval implementation.

## Tech stack

- **React 18, Vite, and i18n:** onboarding workspace and English/Japanese UI.
- **Node.js and Express:** authentication, chat, recall, and service APIs.
- **Python, LangGraph, and LangChain:** retrieval and response orchestration.
- **PostgreSQL, Neo4j, and Redis:** identity and access data, knowledge graphs, and caching.
- **WebRTC and Socket.IO:** realtime avatar interface and communication.
- **Docker Compose, Kubernetes, GCP, and Caddy:** local and production infrastructure.

## Engineering decisions

Answers expose their evidence so a new contributor can verify information instead of trusting an opaque response. Access is scoped by project membership rather than a broad global role, while configurable model and embedding providers keep the core onboarding workflow independent of a single AI vendor.

name: AI PR Review Agent
description: A multi-agent GitHub review system that combines specialist findings, confidence gates, and human approval before posting.
longDescription:
## Overview

AI PR Review Agent reviews a pull request as a small engineering team rather than as one large prompt. Four focused agents inspect security, code quality, tests, and documentation. Their findings are grounded in the repository, merged, scored, and either posted automatically or sent to a human approval queue.

## System architecture

```text
GitHub pull request
        │ webhook + HMAC verification
        ▼
 FastAPI ingress ── deduplication
        │
        ▼
 Redis / ARQ queue ── retry + timeout controls
        │
        ▼
 LangGraph orchestrator
   ┌────┼────────┬────────┐
   ▼    ▼        ▼        ▼
Security Quality Tests   Docs
   └────┴────────┴────────┘
        │ grounded retrieval
        ▼
 Aggregator ── confidence + severity gate
        ├── high confidence ──► GitHub review
        └── uncertain/critical ► Human approval
        │
        ▼
PostgreSQL / TimescaleDB ── events, cost, latency
        │
        ▼
 Next.js monitoring dashboard
```

## How a review moves through the system

1. GitHub sends a signed pull-request webhook to FastAPI. The ingress verifies the raw request and drops duplicate delivery IDs.
2. ARQ places the work on Redis so the webhook can return quickly and failed jobs can be retried safely.
3. LangGraph fans the diff out to four specialist reviewers in parallel. Each reviewer retrieves related repository code using vector and full-text search.
4. The aggregator removes duplicate findings and calculates overall confidence. Critical or uncertain results stop at the human approval gate.
5. Every step emits an event with latency, model usage, and cost, making each review traceable after it runs.

## Tech stack

- **FastAPI and Python:** webhook ingress, validation, and service APIs.
- **LangGraph:** parallel agent orchestration and stateful review flow.
- **Redis and ARQ:** background jobs, retries, and orchestration checkpoints.
- **PostgreSQL, TimescaleDB, and pgvector:** audit events, cost telemetry, full-text search, and vector retrieval.
- **Next.js:** read-only dashboard for repositories, reviews, findings, confidence, and cost.

## Engineering decisions

The system separates specialists so each prompt has a narrow responsibility. It fails closed when cost data or a diff is unavailable, prevents duplicate GitHub comments through idempotency, and keeps humans in control whenever confidence is low or severity is critical.

name: MoneyPlant
description: A Telegram-first personal finance and investment tracker with privacy-aware categorization and a private analytics dashboard.
longDescription:
## Overview

MoneyPlant is a Telegram-first personal finance and investment tracker. A message such as `dinner 1240` becomes a categorized transaction, enters a five-minute correction window, and then appears in a private dashboard with spending and portfolio analytics.

## System architecture

```text
Telegram message                 Web browser
       │                              │
       ▼                              ▼
 grammY bot                     Next.js dashboard
       │                              │
       └──────────┬───────────────────┘
                  ▼
          Shared TypeScript core
     parse amount → mask sensitive data
       → keyword category → AI fallback
                  │
                  ▼
       Five-minute pending state
          ├── edit / cancel
          └── auto-commit
                  │
                  ▼
        Drizzle ORM + PostgreSQL
          ├── transactions
          ├── holdings
          └── user isolation
                  │
        ┌─────────┴─────────┐
        ▼                   ▼
 Spending analytics    AMFI NAV pricing
```

## How an entry moves through the system

1. The Telegram bot receives a short natural-language expense or investment message.
2. A deterministic parser understands Indian amount formats such as `40k`, `1.5L`, and rupee-formatted values.
3. Keyword rules categorize familiar entries without spending an AI call. Ambiguous text is sent to Claude only after the amount is removed.
4. The entry remains pending for five minutes, giving the user time to edit or cancel it before it is committed.
5. The dashboard reads the same PostgreSQL data to provide search, editing, CSV export, spending trends, and investment valuation.

## Tech stack

- **Next.js, Tailwind CSS, and Auth.js:** private dashboard, API routes, and account sessions.
- **grammY:** Telegram bot commands, messages, and secure account linking.
- **TypeScript packages:** shared parsing, categorization, privacy, and finance logic across the bot and web app.
- **PostgreSQL and Drizzle ORM:** transactions, pending entries, holdings, and per-user data isolation.
- **Claude API:** optional fallback for ambiguous categories after sensitive amounts are masked.
- **Bun workspaces and Docker:** monorepo development and self-hosted deployment.

## Engineering decisions

The fast and predictable path stays deterministic; AI is a fallback rather than a dependency. A pending-state window makes chat-based input forgiving, while shared packages prevent the bot and dashboard from implementing different financial rules.

name: RAG Builder
description: A framework-free RAG toolkit tested on 10,000+ page corpora, with custom chunking, local embeddings, and 93% benchmark retrieval accuracy.
longDescription:
## Overview

RAG Builder is a developer-facing retrieval-augmented generation toolkit built from first principles. I implemented the complete indexing and retrieval path without LangChain or a vector database, then tuned chunking and query-time scoring against a reproducible benchmark to reach 93% retrieval accuracy on corpora exceeding 10,000 pages.

## System architecture

```text
                 INDEXING
PDF corpus (10,000+ pages)
     │ PyMuPDF extraction
     ▼
Custom recursive splitter
     │ chunks + source metadata
     ▼
Sentence Transformer
     │ embedding vectors
     ▼
CSV files on local disk

                 QUERYING
User question
     │ same embedding model
     ▼
Question vector
     │ tuned cosine-similarity scoring
     ▼
Ranked source chunks
     │ context + question
     ▼
Local LLM or Gemini API
     │
     ▼
Grounded terminal response
```

## My contribution

I designed and implemented the pipeline end to end: PDF extraction, recursive chunking, embedding generation, CSV persistence, similarity scoring, context assembly, and local/API inference. I also created the benchmark workflow used to tune indexing and retrieval behavior.

## Tech stack

- **Python and PyMuPDF:** corpus ingestion and PDF extraction.
- **Sentence Transformers:** local embedding generation for documents and queries.
- **NumPy and Pandas:** vector scoring, ranking, and inspectable CSV storage.
- **Local models or Gemini:** interchangeable response generation after retrieval.

## Engineering decisions

CSV storage keeps every vector inspectable and removes infrastructure overhead. That choice works well for learning and moderate local corpora; at larger production scale, the linear scan would move to an approximate-nearest-neighbor index while preserving the same chunking and evaluation contracts.

name: Personal Site
description: An Atlas-style personal website for project case studies, public blogs, and private learning logs.
longDescription:
## Overview

This personal site gives projects, technical blogs, and private learning notes one clear home. The interface uses a single Atlas visual system designed for quick navigation by recruiters, collaborators, and technical readers.

## System architecture

```text
Visitor browser
      │
      ▼
Next.js App Router on Vercel
  ├── static pages ─────► Home / About
  ├── project routes ───► versioned JSON content
  └── serverless APIs
          ├── Blogs ─────► MongoDB Atlas
          ├── Logs ──────► authenticated private data
          └── Activity ──► GitHub / coding profiles
      │
      ▼
Responsive Atlas interface
```

## How content is delivered

1. Next.js prerenders the stable portfolio pages for fast first loads.
2. Project case studies live in version-controlled JSON, so updates deploy predictably with the code.
3. Public blogs are loaded from MongoDB Atlas and can be searched or filtered by category.
4. Authentication protects personal learning logs and editing actions.
5. Vercel serves static assets globally and runs API routes only when requested.

## Tech stack

- **Next.js 16 and React 19:** App Router pages, serverless APIs, and image optimization.
- **TypeScript:** shared types and safer application code.
- **MongoDB Atlas and Mongoose:** public blogs and private learning-log persistence.
- **Tailwind CSS and custom CSS:** responsive Atlas design system and interaction states.
- **Vercel:** deployment, previews, static delivery, and serverless execution.

## Engineering decisions

Projects stay in Git because Vercel functions have an ephemeral filesystem, while frequently updated writing belongs in MongoDB. The production build uses one visual identity, a small MongoDB connection pool, and static rendering wherever possible to keep navigation consistent and resource usage low.
